hook: You know David took a census that brought a plague. But did you know Samuel says the LORD moved him to it, and Chronicles says Satan did?
story:
It is one of the darker chapters in David’s life, and the Bible tells it twice.

2 Samuel opens it like this: “Again the LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them”. The order follows: “Go, count Israel and Judah.”

1 Chronicles opens the same story another way: “Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel.”

Same king, same census, and in Hebrew the same verb for moved. But in Samuel the sentence makes the LORD, whose anger burned against Israel, the one who moved David. In Chronicles it is Satan.

The two chapters differ in some numbers too, and those are real differences, but the sharpest one stands in the first line. So the question is fair. Who moved David to count Israel, God or the adversary? And if it was God, how could the census be David’s sin?

moment:
The word “Again” points back. Earlier there had been “a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year”. Now David orders Joab, the captain of his army, to go “from Dan even to Beersheba, and count the people, that I may know the sum of the people.”

Joab pushes back: “But why does my lord the king delight in this thing?” In Chronicles he adds, “Why will he be a cause of guilt to Israel?” The king overrules him, and Chronicles names what Joab felt: “the king’s word was abominable to Joab.” He leaves Levi and Benjamin out of the count.

The counting takes “nine months and twenty days”. Then, before any judgment is announced, “David’s heart struck him”. He tells the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in that which I have done.”

Neither book spells out exactly what made the census a sin. The law of Moses attached a ransom to every census, “that there be no plague among them when you count them”, and Chronicles remembers that the LORD had promised to increase Israel “like the stars of the sky.” Commentators have suggested pride, trust in the size of an army, or distrust of that promise.
around:
The prophet Gad brings David three choices. David answers, “I am in distress. Let us fall now into the LORD’s hand, for his mercies are great. Let me not fall into man’s hand.” A plague follows, and “seventy thousand men died”. When the angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem, “the LORD relented of the disaster” and says, “It is enough. Now withdraw your hand.” David, seeing the angel, pleads for the people: “these sheep, what have they done?”

The two accounts differ in other details as well. Samuel counts “eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword” in Israel and “five hundred thousand” in Judah; Chronicles has “one million one hundred thousand men” and “four hundred seventy thousand”. Samuel’s prophet offers “seven years of famine”, Chronicles’ “three years of famine”. Samuel says David paid “fifty shekels of silver” for the threshing floor and the oxen; Chronicles says “six hundred shekels of gold by weight for the place.” These are real differences too. This page is about the first verse.
after:
David bought the threshing floor and refused to take it as a gift: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God which cost me nothing.” He built an altar, and Chronicles says the LORD answered him “from the sky by fire on the altar of burnt offering.” David “was afraid because of the sword of the LORD’s angel”, and he said of that place, “This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel.”

He was right about the place. His son Solomon built the temple “on Mount Moriah”, “on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.” It is the same name as the land where Abraham had once been sent with Isaac, “the land of Moriah”. The place where the plague stopped became the place of the house of God.

Matthew Henry later noticed what Chronicles chose to tell. It leaves out David’s sin with Uriah, but it tells this one, because in the atonement for it the place of the temple was shown. And the first verse of the story became a test case for how to read the Bible itself.
readings:
Readers have explained the two openings in several ways.

Many Christian commentators read them together: God allowed what the adversary did, and Scripture often speaks of God doing what he permits. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown put it that way, with James 1:13 in view, and so does Ellicott’s note on Samuel. The Bible has similar scenes. In Job the LORD tells Satan, “Behold, all that he has is in your power.” In 1 Kings a spirit stands before the LORD and says, “I will entice him.”

A second reading looks at the Hebrew word. Satan means adversary, and in Chronicles it stands without the article. The same word is used of human opponents: “The LORD raised up an adversary to Solomon”. Barnes therefore read it as some person who urged David on. Ellicott’s note on Chronicles took the adversary to be God’s own wrath, and suggests that the word may once have stood in Samuel too and fallen out in copying. Bible Hub’s Hebrew lexicon, for its part, lists this verse as the proper name Satan.

A third reading says the two books really differ. The Jewish Encyclopedia holds that the Chronicler, writing long after the book of Samuel and drawing on it, saw Satan as an independent agent, while the older books referred everything, good or bad, to God, as when “an evil spirit from the LORD troubled” Saul. It adds that Persian ideas may have played a part, and calls that a possibility.

None of these readings has settled the matter for everyone.
argued:
This pair of verses has been used for a long time to argue about how to read the Bible itself.

Joseph Benson took Chronicles as the key to Samuel. Without the second account, he argued, a reader might have concluded from 2 Samuel 24:1 that God pushes people into sin, and he drew a rule from that: [[benson]]

Albert Barnes went another way. Reading the Hebrew word in Chronicles as a plain noun, an adversary, he looked for a human hand behind the census: [[barnes]]

The Jewish Encyclopedia saw not a key but a change between an older book and a later one: [[jacobs-blau]]

So the same two verses serve one reader as proof that Scripture explains Scripture, and another as evidence that its writers saw the ways of God differently over time.
point: Read alone, 2 Samuel 24:1 can sound as if God pushed David into a sin and then punished it. Read beside Chronicles, the same event is told from two sides: one names the LORD’s anger against Israel, the other an adversary standing against Israel. The Bible keeps both openings. However readers fit them together, both books agree on the rest: David insisted against Joab’s advice, said that he had sinned, and paid the full price for the place where the plague stopped.
lesson:
When something goes wrong in your life, it is natural to ask who pushed you there. God? The enemy? The people around you? These two chapters do not answer every part of that question. But look at what David does.

He does not blame Joab, or the adversary, or God. He says, “I have sinned greatly in that which I have done.” When the plague comes, he asks that the hand fall on him and his family, not on the people: “these sheep, what have they done?” And when Araunah offers him everything for nothing, he says no. He will not offer to God what costs him nothing.

If you are carrying something you did, you could begin where David began: name it before God without passing it on to anyone else, and let your turning back cost you something real. Read 2 Samuel 24 and 1 Chronicles 21 side by side, and notice where the story ends: at an altar, on the ground where the temple would later stand.

And if you do not share this faith, the story still holds something worth hearing: a leader who owns his failure instead of passing it on to others.

echoes.note: James draws the line many readers bring to this chapter: “God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.” The pull toward wrong comes from a person’s own desire.
This psalm puts into words what David did after the census: “I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity.”
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins”. Confession, not blame, is where the way back begins, as it was for David.
